extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians preparing research papers for publication (especially novice authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing, typesetting (LaTeX), structuring, and preparing mathematical research articles for publication and electronic distribution, aimed at authors preparing manuscripts for journals and archives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract and introduction as main selling points
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract and the introduction are the main 'selling points' of a paper; many readers will decide whether to read further based on them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indirect 'advertising' is necessary because many papers will not be read; prepare a clear, informative abstract and an engaging introduction to attract readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit files in absolutely final form
rubrics_metrics.description: Files must be prepared with extreme care and submitted in absolutely final form as regards mathematical content, notation, language and sometimes TeX typesetting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers have reduced in-house work; authors are often required to do tasks previously done by publishers. Also: thoroughly check page proofs prepared by the publisher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer journals that publish electronic versions
rubrics_metrics.description: The electronic version of an article is increasingly important and may become the only published form; avoid submitting to journals that do not publish electronic versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider future discoverability and accessibility when choosing a journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare manuscripts for computerized/automated submission systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Because submission and production processes are often automated, prepare manuscripts meticulously to avoid exceptional situations that automated systems cannot handle (e.g., late corrections or withdrawal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on human intervention; ensure files and metadata are complete and conform to the journal's required formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think of a specific reader
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing, think of a (specific) reader — a mathematician who can understand the text completely but does not work on exactly the same subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain definitions the reader may not know; explain why fragments are important or worth reading; omit what the reader considers trivial; keep the reader from becoming bored or irritated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write grammatical English and respect the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical papers ought to be written in grammatical (not necessarily idiomatic) English; good language is a form of respecting the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather examples by British/American mathematical writers in your area; write directly in English where possible (don't translate); avoid copying from previous papers or non-native advisers; check new words in a dictionary; avoid fancy or witty language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain two LaTeX source files: archival and publisher
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep one source file for your archive (with comments, omitted fragments, many macros) and a separate cleaned-up final file for the publisher containing only needed macros.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare the publisher file in the form required by the publisher; keep the archival file for development and notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not adopt a journal-specific style early; use standard document classes
rubrics_metrics.description: When starting, do not use the style of a specific journal; instead use standard styles (e.g., amsart or article) and reformat only at the final stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use amsart for \\address, \\keywords, \\subjclass; if using article add appropriate packages (amsmath, amssymb).

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep LaTeX code simple; use standard constructions and avoid problematic environments
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple formula should have simple code; use standard LaTeX constructions; do not reinvent LaTeX or use constructions known to cause issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: type a(x+y)^2 rather than elaborate spacing commands; use \frac{1}{2} with braces when needed; avoid eqnarray (use align instead). Use standard preamble definitions rather than ad hoc constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use macros for repeated complicated notation but avoid publisher-side macros for LaTeX commands
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce macros for frequently used complicated symbols or parameterized notation to make global changes easy; however, in the publisher file avoid macros that abbreviate LaTeX commands (e.g., \be for \begin{equation}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: \newcommand{\tcS}{\widetilde\mathcal{S}}; parameterized macros like \newcommand{\row}[2]{#1_1,\ldots,#1_{#2}}; delimited macros (\def\<#1>{\langle#1\rangle}) are useful but know their limits (nested cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Label references; never hard-code numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not write fixed numbers like 'By (5), (12) and Theorem 3.1'; instead use \label and \ref to refer to numbered items so numbers update automatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt label naming conventions by object type (e.g., \label{T:Pythagoras}, \label{L:Kurat-Zorn}, \label{E:tr.ineq.}); use showkeys (e.g., \usepackage[nocite]{showkeys}) during writing to display labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only number objects that are referred to
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects and displayed formulas that are not referred to later need not be numbered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use unnumbered versions for such items (e.g., \newtheorem*{xrem}{Remark} or \[ ... \] for unnumbered displays). Numbering only referenced items reduces clutter.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to display a formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Display formulas that are long (longer than ~3/4 of text width), have high elements (fractions, matrices, sums, integrals), contain definitions used later, or when there are two analogous formulas in a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not display short formulas the reader will not need to return to; avoid repeating the same displayed formula twice; use displayed formulas to aid readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inline math conventions: keep punctuation and spaces outside $...$
rubrics_metrics.description: In undisplayed text, put only mathematics within the $ signs; leave punctuation marks and spaces outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: write 'the polynomials $x+1$, $x^2+1$, $x^3-2$' rather than 'the polynomials $x+1, x^2+1, x^3-2$' to ensure spacing and linebreaks are correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'touching' formulas; put words between inline formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Inline formulas should not 'touch' other formulas too often; insert words to clarify logical roles and reduce reader confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of improved wording are provided (e.g., 'Since x = 2, it follows that x^2 = 4' instead of 'Since x = 2, x^2 = 4'). Slightly longer sentences can improve readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use itemize/enumerate to clarify complex logical structure; choose numbering style carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Use list environments for sequences of statements; choose numbering formats that don't conflict with formula numbers and are convenient to cite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can use \item[\textrm{(a)}] to force labels, or the enumerate package (e.g., \begin{enumerate}[\upshape (i)]). Itemized structures can make complicated sentences intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid close repetitions and warn if reusing similar text or proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Copying and pasting similar fragments can confuse readers; if similar formulations are necessary, either indicate concise differences or warn the reader before repeating a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example phrasing: 'The statement of (i) remains true with "bounded" replaced by "unbounded"...' or 'We now mimic the proof of Lemma 2.3 with appropriate adjustments in the constants.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use correct accents and encoding for names
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing names in different languages, always add appropriate accents and use correct font encoding (e.g., \usepackage[T1]{fontenc}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to encode Polish characters properly; ensures names are presented accurately in references and text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title should indicate the branch and be concise and specific
rubrics_metrics.description: A good title should indicate the branch of mathematics, should not be too long or too general, and should avoid abbreviations or complicated symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stylistic devices that can work: question titles, complete-sentence statements of main results, or verbal/gerund forms (e.g., 'Computing the eigenvalues of M-matrices'). Avoid macros in titles because publishers may extract titles automatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place acknowledgements at the end, not on first pages
rubrics_metrics.description: Put thanks, grant acknowledgements, etc., at the end of the paper (before References) in a \subsection*{Acknowledgements} rather than decorating the author/title with asterisks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This saves space on the first pages, which influence whether a reader reads more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract should state main results clearly, concisely, and independently
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal aim of the abstract is to present the main results (theorems); it should be short (one paragraph), avoid empty phrases, be independent of the paper (no references to theorem numbers), and avoid macros and \cite's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If possible, formulate the theorem so it can be stated without a blackboard and repeat it in the abstract; the abstract may include advertising elements like 'We improve a result of Kowalski [..]'. Avoid complicated formulas in the abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction: include interesting content, main results, and literature discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Only include what is interesting; two elements that should always appear are your theorems and a discussion of relevant literature. Main results should be transportable to the introduction after possibly a few definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convince the reader you know related work and compare your results with others; avoid long lists of unrelated references; do not start with a long list of definitions and notations; the first paragraph should arrest the reader's attention; in long papers you may include sketches, logical schemes, or suggestions for further research.

rubrics_metrics.name: References must be complete, accurate, and extracted from original sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide complete bibliographic information (page numbers, publisher, editors for volumes) and ensure items labeled 'preprint' are checked for publication; extract data from the original items or verified databases (MathSciNet, Zentralblatt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For contributed volumes give the actual title of the volume, place and date of conference, publisher, editors; note that publication date may differ from conference date. As a rule, list a paper only if it is cited in the text; avoid an excessive proportion of self-citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulate theorems precisely: sentences without free variables and in imperative mood
rubrics_metrics.description: A theorem is a sentence without free variables — it is either true or not; use imperative wording and do not put fragments of the proof into the theorem statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example styles: 'Every finite group is...', 'If... then...'; avoid phrases like 'we shall prove that the theorem holds for k=1' — instead state 'we shall prove that the conclusion of the theorem holds for k=1.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions: emphasize the defined term and use clear definition markers
rubrics_metrics.description: In definitions, emphasize the term being defined (e.g., with \emph{...}) and use notation := or =: to indicate which side is being defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'We define the convex hull of E to be the smallest convex set containing E.' Or 'Then F = abcde + f ghi =: A + B.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof writing: consider reader competence; omit obvious steps and be clear about what is proved
rubrics_metrics.description: A reader of a proof is competent and concentrated; omit arguments obvious to every mathematician and avoid long lists of references which may obscure the reasoning. Make clear for each statement whether it has been proved, will be proved, or the reader is to supply the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concise expressions (e.g., write 'Then |a| ≤ |a−b| + |b−c|' instead of 'Then, by the triangle inequality,...'); for similar cases you may write 'The analysis of case (b) is similar and left to the reader.' If necessary, announce proofs ('We now prove that (12) implies A = B. To see this,...'). You may refer readers to supplementary material on a website for complete details.
